explanations.explanation: Three thousand it is. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" and goes looking for David and his men (1 Samuel 24:2). That's a LOT of sandals on one dusty road.

Close on the digits, friend, but the text says three thousand. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" (1 Samuel 24:2). You were off by a whole zero, and that zero is about twenty-seven hundred extra men.

Ten thousand would be a mighty big crowd, but the text says three thousand. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" (1 Samuel 24:2). Still plenty of men to go after David and his group.

David and his men, hiding in the recesses of the cave (1 Samuel 24:3). Saul has come out looking for them (1 Samuel 24:2), and now he's walking into the very cave where they are. I bet that was the quietest bunch of grown men ever.

Saul did just come back from pursuing the Philistines (1 Samuel 24:1), so I see why that one came to mind. But the ones hiding in the cave are "…David and his men…" (1 Samuel 24:3). The Philistines aren't in this cave at all.

The text doesn't put anybody from Keilah in this scene. It says "…David and his men were hiding in the recesses of the cave." (1 Samuel 24:3). Those are the ones in the cave. Saul had gone out to look for David and his men (1 Samuel 24:2).

Enemy is right. David's men say, "This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ’Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish.’…" (1 Samuel 24:4). They say it with Saul in the cave. Then David creeps up, and what he does next surprises everybody.
A kingdom is a big gift, but that's not the word in the quote. The men say the LORD told David, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand…" (1 Samuel 24:4). The word is enemy.
Not people, friend. The words David's men repeat are, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish." (1 Samuel 24:4). It's the enemy being delivered.

explanations.answer: Cuts off a corner of Saul's robe
explanations.explanation: David "…stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:4). It's a small snip, and it leads to a big moment. Keep an eye on that little piece of cloth, because it comes back.

explanations.answer: Takes the sword from Saul's side
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention Saul's sword in this scene. David "…stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:4). Later he points Saul to that very corner of cloth (1 Samuel 24:11). So the robe is the thing to remember, not any sword.

explanations.answer: Unties the straps of Saul's sandals
explanations.explanation: No sandal straps here. The text says David "…stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:4). The robe is where all the action is.

Not quite, friend. The text says "Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:5). After the snip, his heart bothered him. He didn't walk away proud of it, and I think that says a lot about David.

False is right. "Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:5). After the snip, his heart bothered him. That's a tender heart over one little corner of cloth.
Anointed is right. David says, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). That's the reason he gives his men, plain and simple.

Servant is a fine word, but it's not the one David uses. He tells his men, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). That's David's reason, and he gives it right after his conscience bothers him (1 Samuel 24:5). The word that holds his reason is anointed.

Champion sounds mighty, but David's reason isn't about Saul's strength. He tells his men, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). His men had just told him this was the day (1 Samuel 24:4). The word that holds his answer is anointed.

True. "With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul." (1 Samuel 24:7). Those men had just said this was the day the LORD spoke of. David answered them with words, and the men did not rise up.
Not false, friend. The text says "With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul." (1 Samuel 24:7). David stopped them with his words.

explanations.answer: Leaves the cave and goes on his way
explanations.explanation: That's it. "Then Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). Behind him, David had just cut off a corner of his robe (1 Samuel 24:4) and held his men back. The text doesn't say Saul noticed anything yet. Hold onto that, because David is about to step out of that cave.

explanations.answer: Calls his chosen men into the cave
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Saul calls anybody in. It says "…Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). He just walks out.

explanations.answer: Lies down to sleep in the cave
explanations.explanation: No nap for Saul. The text says "…Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). With David's men in the back, a nap would have been quite the plot twist.

David calls out, "My lord the king!" and then "…David bowed facedown in reverence…" (1 Samuel 24:8). Saul looks behind him and sees a man on his face in the dirt. I think a bow like that shows David's respect for Saul.
The text has no sword in David's hand here. It says "…David bowed facedown in reverence…" (1 Samuel 24:8). He greets the king with a bow.
David doesn't run. He walks out and "…bowed facedown in reverence…" (1 Samuel 24:8). He's done hiding for this conversation.

Harm is right. David asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ’Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). I think he's asking Saul to think about who he's listening to. Then he points Saul to what happened in the cave.

Mock isn't the word. David asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ’Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). The men David mentions say he means to harm the king. That's the word that fills the blank.
Desert doesn't show up in David's question. He says, "Look, David intends to harm you…" (1 Samuel 24:9). Harm is the word.

True. David says, "I was told to kill you, but I spared you…" (1 Samuel 24:10). He tells Saul straight out how close it came. Then he points to the robe corner and says, "…I cut it off, but I did not kill you." (1 Samuel 24:11).
Not false, friend. David tells Saul, "I was told to kill you, but I spared you…" (1 Samuel 24:10). He's being honest about how close it got.

Rebellion is right. David tells Saul, "…look at the corner of your robe in my hand." (1 Samuel 24:11). Then he adds, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). He cut the cloth, but he did not kill the king.

Fear isn't in that sentence. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). He's talking about what his hands have done. He cut the robe, but he did not kill Saul, and rebellion fills the blank.

Pride isn't the word here. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). His point is that his hands did not strike the king. Evil and rebellion are the two he names.

Not quite, friend. David says, "May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you." (1 Samuel 24:12). He leaves the judging to the LORD.

False is right. David says, "May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you." (1 Samuel 24:12). He puts it in the LORD's hands, not his own.

explanations.answer: A dead dog and a flea
explanations.explanation: A dead dog and a flea. David asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). He's calling himself small. I've been called a lot of things in my day, but never a flea.

Those are big, scary animals, and David doesn't use them here. He asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). I think he's showing Saul how little there is to chase. A dead dog and a flea are small and low, nothing like a lion or a bear.
Those are gentle little creatures, but David doesn't name them. He asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). He's making himself sound small.

Saul's hand. David prays, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). He's speaking to Saul while he asks the LORD to plead his case. I think that's a bold way to pray with the king standing right there.
The Philistines aren't in David's prayer. He asks the LORD to "…deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15), and he's talking to Saul. So the hand is Saul's.
David's men aren't named in that prayer. He asks the LORD to "…deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15), talking to Saul. So it's Saul's hand.
Son is right. Saul calls back, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David said "my father," and Saul answers with "my son."

Servant isn't what Saul says. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David had called him "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11), and Saul answers with a family word too. The word is son.

Friend is a nice word, but Saul uses another. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David had called him "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11), so Saul answers in the same family way. Then Saul weeps aloud.

explanations.answer: You are more righteous than I
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Saul tells David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). That's a hard thing for anyone to say out loud.

explanations.answer: You have fooled me once again
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't say that. After weeping, he says, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). He takes David's side.

That's not what Saul says here. After weeping aloud, he says, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). He's talking about what David did for him. Trust doesn't come up in that sentence.

True. Saul says, "May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day." (1 Samuel 24:19). Just a couple of verses earlier he said David had rewarded him with good (1 Samuel 24:17). Now he asks the LORD to reward David too.

Not false, friend. Saul really does say, "May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day." (1 Samuel 24:19). Earlier he said David had rewarded him with good (1 Samuel 24:17), so now he asks the same for David. I think hearing that from Saul would surprise anybody.

King is right. Saul says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). He says it himself, right there in the wilderness.

Priest isn't the word. Saul says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king…" (1 Samuel 24:20). He goes on to say that "…the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). That's the work of a king.

Judge isn't what Saul says. He says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king…" (1 Samuel 24:20). Then he adds that the kingdom of Israel "…will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). The word he uses is king.

explanations.answer: Not to cut off his descendants
explanations.explanation: That's what Saul asks. He says, "…swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). It's a request about his family line. He asks it right after saying David will be king (1 Samuel 24:20).

explanations.answer: Never to come near his house
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't ask for that. He says, "…swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). He asks that his descendants and his name be kept. He doesn't ask David to stay away.

explanations.answer: To fight the Philistines for him
explanations.explanation: The Philistines don't come up in Saul's request. He asks David to swear "…that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). Saul is asking about his family line. He wants his descendants and his name kept.
Not so, friend. The text says "…David gave his oath to Saul." (1 Samuel 24:22). He didn't refuse. He gave it.
False is right. "…David gave his oath to Saul." (1 Samuel 24:22). He gave Saul what he asked for.
Up to the stronghold. "…Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). They each go their own way.
Keilah isn't named here. The text says "…David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). Saul heads home, and David goes the other way, up to the stronghold. They split up.
The cave is behind them now. The text says "…David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). They go up higher.
